sources.title: Brandon Seale, “Lipan Apache Indians,” Handbook of Texas
sources.note: Lines 6 to 17 and 60 to 84: Southern Athabaskan identity, archaeological chronology, alliance-making, decentralized leadership, diaspora, continuity, recognition, and distinct modern organizations.

sources.title: National Park Service, “Apaches (1450 AD to 1700 AD)”
sources.note: Lines 21 to 30: broad Apache, not specifically Lipan, movement around 1500; 1541 Querechos; bison, dogs, tools, water containers, fuel, horses, and later dispersal.

sources.title: Texas Department of Transportation, TxDOT Tribal Histories: Mescalero Apache Tribe Research Report
sources.note: PDF page 11, Table 1: Kónitsąą or Kónitsąą-hii is listed for Lipan Apache people / People of Big Water; the table separately lists subgroup names and cites Hoijer 1975.

sources.title: Lipan Apache Tribe, “Timeline of the Lipan Apache Tribe, 17th - 21st Centuries”
sources.note: Lines 30 to 32, 47, and 54: community chronology for circa 1600 to 1670 arrival, identity, trade, divisions, drought, and horses, plus the separately dated 1750 and 1780 smallpox entries and the 1780 peyote-healing account.

sources.title: Instituto Nacional de Lenguas Indígenas, “Lengua N'dee/N'nee/Ndé”
sources.note: Published June 5, 2023, sections Territorio, Datos lingüísticos, and Grado de riesgo: Na-Dené classification, Ndé miizaa as the Lipan variety, writing-system review, interrupted transmission, and community-based revitalization.

sources.title: Nancy McGown Minor, “Our Language: The Meaning of Our Apache Name ‘Lipan’”
sources.note: Lines 24 to 32: official tribal-history interpretation of łépai plus indeh or ndé as “The Light Gray People,” dated January 10, 2009.

sources.title: Nancy McGown Minor, “Our Sacred History: The Lipan Apache Bands”
sources.note: Lines 24 to 55: retrospective account of divisions, 10 to 14 bands, rancherías as extended-family groups, leadership, unity, and named bands including Kúne tsá.

sources.title: Nancy McGown Minor, “Everyday Life in Lipan Past”
sources.note: Lines 24 to 32: community account of later bison hunts, reunions, marriages, hunting practice, women’s gathering and basketry, plant foods, and riverbank corn and squash.

sources.title: Nancy McGown Minor, “The Lipan Homeland of Many Houses (kíłááhíí)”
sources.note: Lines 24 to 36, especially 29 to 34: community-history account of seventeenth-century movement into Texas, resources sought, later southward movement, Kíłááhíí around San Antonio, and Naa-ci-ká in Coahuila.

sources.title: Robert Soto, “Lipan Apache Musical Lyrics: Vocable Sounds and English Translation”
sources.note: PDF page 1, lines 0 to 10: contributor, May 2014 date, exact Lipan lines and English translations; “Nii gooyí” is translated “There is a good land.”

sources.title: Ashley Leal, “The Lipan Apaches,” in Native American Peoples of South Texas
sources.note: Printed pages 45 to 52, PDF pages 52 to 59, especially printed pages 46 to 48, PDF pages 53 to 55: food, dwellings, smoke opening, clothing by age, horse adoption, and travel burdens.

sources.title: Ashley S. Leal, The Lipan Apache (Ndé) Tribe of Texas Powwow: A Curriculum of Culture(S) and Pedagogy of Place
sources.note: Lines 19 to 60: 2024 tribal-member ethnography, interviews, cultural survival, community connectedness, and powwow as local knowledge transmission.

sources.title: Texas Beyond History, “Apache,” Plateaus and Canyonlands
sources.note: Lines 23 to 34 and 65 to 92: Apache naming and source cautions, later food and housing, close-knit matrilineal families, grandparents’ teaching, work, crafts, healing, and mourning.

sources.title: Texas Beyond History, “Mission San Lorenzo de la Santa Cruz”
sources.note: Lines 1 to 18 and 27 to 38: 1762 to 1771 colonial mission, buildings, irrigation, middens, trade goods, Native crafts, burials, food remains, and artifact locators.

sources.title: National Park Service, “Mission Santa Cruz de San Sabá and Presidio San Luis de las Amarillas”
sources.note: Lines 34 to 72: 1757 mission, Lipan alliance strategy, refusal to settle, bison hunting, 1758 attack, archaeology, and Spanish irrigation ditch.

sources.title: National Park Service, “Comanche Lookout”
sources.note: Lines 41 to 46 and 67 to 71: site evidence, older travel routes, Lipan horse expansion, broad later Apache control claim, and displacement chronology with citations.

sources.title: Lipan Apache Tribe, “About Our Treaties”
sources.note: Lines 24 to 104: official community list of treaties with Spain, Mexico, Republic of Texas, United States, and other nations from 1749 to 1865.

sources.title: “1822 Bustamante Treaty with the Lipan Apache”
sources.note: PDF pages 1 to 6; Articles 1 to 8 and appended transcription record peace, movement, trade, water and pasture access, wild-horse gathering, and named Lipan negotiators.

sources.title: Lipan Apache Tribe, “Our Sacred History: Who We Are”
sources.note: Lines 24 to 45, especially 29 to 34: community account of migration, divisions, epidemics, food shortages, dispersal, elders teaching children, surviving enclaves, a united present-day tribal organization, government, and continuity.

sources.title: Lipan Apache Tribe, “Frequently Asked Questions”
sources.note: Lines 24 to 69: descent-based enrollment, elders and family records, current non-federal status, scholarships, possible health-service limits, social learning, and language restoration.

sources.title: Nancy McGown Minor, “The Story of Kesetta and Jack”
sources.note: Lines 24 to 32 and notes: children captured from a Lipan camp in 1877; the page explicitly disputes uncertain dates, kinship, and leadership claims in later retellings.

sources.title: Smithsonian Institution, “MS 81 Lipan Apache Vocabulary”
sources.note: Collection record: A. S. Gatschet vocabulary from Fort Griffin, Texas, September to October 1884, about 46 used pages with words and some phrases and sentences.

sources.title: Morris E. Opler, “The Use of Peyote by the Carrizo and Lipan Apache Tribes”
sources.note: Lines 23 to 44 and 74 to 116: exact title, author, American Anthropologist volume 40, 1938 date, pages 271 to 285, and DOI.

sources.title: Texas Historical Commission, “Cementerio del Barrio de los Lipanes” marker text
sources.note: PDF page 51, lines 1373 to 1399: sacred cemetery, 1790s peace settlement, bands, descendants on both sides of the border, 45 identified graves, markers, and 2021 designation.

sources.title: Lipan Apache Tribe, “About the Lipan Apache Tribe Cemetery Association (LATCA)”
sources.note: Lines 24 to 46, especially 26 and 35 to 46: association purpose, Presidio cemetery status, community preservation, transfers, and repatriations through November 2025.

sources.title: Texas Legislature, “S.C.R. No. 61,” Senate Concurrent Resolution
sources.note: PDF pages 1 to 2, lines 25 to 73: 2019 resolution recognizes the Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas and records government, community, service, and contributions.

sources.title: National Park Service, “Land and Water Acknowledgement,” San Antonio Missions
sources.note: Lines 22 to 35: distinct peoples, living descendants, federally recognized associated nations, non-federally recognized San Antonio groups including Lipan Apache, and enduring place ties.

sources.title: Lipan Apache Tribe, “Nonprofits of the Tribe”
sources.note: Lines 24 to 60, especially 35 to 50 and 59 to 60: distinction between the Tribe and nonprofit instrumentalities, with stated cultural, educational, health, land, language, cemetery, and public-learning purposes.

sources.title: Nancy McGown Minor, “Dwindling Resources/Economic Cycle”
sources.note: Lines 24 to 31: community account of mixed subsistence, hide trade, horses-for-guns networks, horse breaking, later cash trade, and cross-border alliances.

sources.title: Nancy McGown Minor, “Weapons of the Lipan Apache”
sources.note: Lines 24 to 35: retrospective details for later bows, arrows, children’s arrows, flint-to-metal change, quivers, lances, firearms, and uncertain war-club adoption.

sources.title: Nancy McGown Minor, “Transition- The Reservation and Assimilation”
sources.note: Lines 24 to 31: community account of 1850 smallpox, Mescalero and other destinations, refuge in Mexico, returns, hidden Texas residence, surnames, and Tejano communities.

sources.title: Nancy McGown Minor, “Short Biographies of Some Notable Lipan Chiefs”
sources.note: Lines 24 to 75: explicitly non-exhaustive later leaders; dated diplomacy, trade, kinship alliances, movement, and descendants at Mescalero.

sources.title: Lipan Apache Women Defense, “Letter of Protest to Valley Morning Star Article: ‘Ranches of Significance’”
sources.note: January 30, 2012 post, paragraph beginning “I am the daughter”: a Lipan community author translates Kónitsąąįį gokíyaa as “Big Water Lipan Country” and labels it a traditional territory or homeland.

proposedOverrides.name: Ndé Kónitsąąíí Gokíyaa (Lipan Apache atlas homeland)
proposedOverrides.summary: Approximate 1492 to 1500 overlapping atlas homeland layer paired with carefully dated Southern Athabaskan, Lipan, community, archaeological, and living-continuity evidence.
